blocks.text: Redis is an in-memory data-structure server. It's single-threaded for command execution (I/O threads exist in newer versions), which makes every command atomic and makes it very fast — ~100k+ simple ops per second per core with sub-millisecond latency. It's commonly used as a cache, but its data structures make it a toolkit for rate limiters, leaderboards, queues, locks, sessions and pub/sub.
It isn't a durable primary database by default: data lives in RAM, persistence is optional and asynchronous, and replication is asynchronous, so acknowledged writes can be lost on failover.

head: Type
Commands
Use it for
rows: Leaderboards, time-ordered feeds, sliding-window rate limits, delay queues
Durable-ish event log with consumer groups
Nearby search on a sorted set of geohashes

blocks.text:
ZINCRBY game:42:scores 50 "player:alice"     # add points
ZREVRANGE game:42:scores 0 9 WITHSCORES       # top 10
ZREVRANK game:42:scores "player:alice"        # alice's rank (0-based)
ZREVRANGE game:42:scores 95 105               # players around rank 100
Sorted sets are skip lists plus a hash map, so updates and rank queries are O(log n). A leaderboard with 10M players fits in a few GB and answers rank queries in microseconds.

sections.title: Example: a lock — and its limits

blocks.text:
SET lock:order:123 <random-token> NX PX 30000   # acquire if absent, 30 s TTL
# ... do work ...
# release only if we still own it (Lua for atomicity):
if redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1]) end

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Treating a Redis lock as a correctness guarantee. A GC pause or network delay can outlast the TTL, so two clients may both think they hold it. For correctness, the protected resource must check a fencing token (monotonic number) — or use a consensus-backed lock (etcd, ZooKeeper).

cols.title: RDB snapshots
cons: Lose everything since the last snapshot

items: Replication is asynchronous: primary → replicas. **Sentinel** monitors and fails over a primary/replica set.

**Redis Cluster** shards keys into 16,384 hash slots across primaries, each with replicas. Multi-key commands must hit one slot — use hash tags: `{user:42}:cart` and `{user:42}:profile` land together.
`WAIT n` can make a write wait for n replicas, narrowing (not eliminating) the loss window.

sections.title: How Redis Cluster routes a command

items: **Big keys** (a 10M-element set) block the single thread on delete or scan — use UNLINK and keep collections bounded.
**Hot keys** concentrate load on one shard — replicate or split them.
**O(n) commands** (KEYS *, SMEMBERS on huge sets) stall everything; use SCAN.
**Memory:** set `maxmemory` and an eviction policy, or Redis returns errors when full.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Redis gives me atomic operations on rich data structures in memory — I'd use sorted sets for the leaderboard and a Lua script for the rate limiter — but I'd keep the source of truth in a durable database.
